questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Two Systems That Set the Time of Sleep
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two-process model of sleep
questions.stem: Marine biologist Kira asks which two processes regulate sleep timing and depth.

options.text: Circadian process and homeostatic sleep drive.
REM process and NREM process only.
options.misconception: confuses sleep stages with regulatory processes

options.text: Melatonin process and cortisol process only.
Memory process and emotion process only.
options.misconception: confuses cognitive functions with sleep regulation

questions.explanation: The two-process model posits a circadian process and a homeostatic sleep drive. Stages, hormones, and cognitive functions are not the regulatory processes.

Performance improves as sleepiness plateaus.
Reaction time is unaffected by sleep restriction.

questions.explanation: Objective performance keeps worsening while subjective sleepiness plateaus, so self-report underestimates impairment. Performance does not improve.

questions.stem: Marine biologist Vera reads a prevalence estimate of 10 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of 8 to 12 percent.

options.text: The true prevalence is certainly 10 percent.
The interval width means the sample was too large.
The interval means the estimate is invalid.
The true prevalence likely falls between 8 and 12 percent.

questions.explanation: A 95 percent confidence interval of 8 to 12 percent means the true value likely lies in that range. It does not imply certainty, invalidity, or excessive sample size.
questions.hint: What does a confidence interval represent?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Ratios From a Study That Chose Its Groups
questions.learningObjective: Explain selection bias impact on ratios
questions.stem: Marine biologist Will asks how selecting only severe cases affects an odds ratio in a sleep study.

answer.exemplar: Selecting only severe cases inflates the odds ratio by excluding mild cases, exaggerating the association between exposure and outcome.

questions.explanation: Restricting to severe cases removes mild outcomes, inflating the odds ratio and exaggerating the exposure-outcome association.
questions.hint: Connect case selection to odds ratio inflation.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Two Systems That Set the Time of Sleep
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the circadian sleep propensity minimum
questions.stem: If circadian sleep propensity peaks at 3 a.m. and the wake maintenance zone ends at 9 p.m., how many hours apart are they?
questions.explanation: From 9 p.m. to 3 a.m. is 6 hours. The wake maintenance zone and circadian sleep propensity peak are 6 hours apart.
questions.hint: Count hours from 9 p.m. to 3 a.m.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Self-Report Against Task Performance During Sleep Restriction
questions.stem: Marine biologist Xena must choose the best assessment strategy for sleep restriction effects.

options.text: Rely solely on self-report questionnaires.
Use only a single reaction-time trial.
options.misconception: one trial lacks reliability and sensitivity

options.text: Combine objective performance tests with self-report.
Avoid measurement and rely on appearance.
options.misconception: appearance is not a valid measure

questions.explanation: Combining objective tests with self-report captures both measured impairment and perceived sleepiness. Either alone is insufficient.
questions.hint: Which option uses both measurement types?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Whether Recovery Sleep Restores Everything
questions.learningObjective: Identify a non-restored function after recovery
questions.stem: Marine biologist Yves asks which function is least restored by a single recovery night after chronic restriction.

options.text: Basic alertness.
Subjective sleepiness.
Simple reaction time.
Executive function and complex decision-making.

questions.explanation: Executive function and complex decision-making recover least after a single recovery night. Alertness, simple RT, and sleepiness improve more readily.
questions.hint: Which function is most cognitively demanding?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: A Night Without Dreaming After a Week Without Sleep
questions.stem: Marine biologist Zara reads that REM rebound is most prominent in the latter half of the recovery night.

options.text: REM rebound is most prominent in the latter half of the night.
REM rebound occurs only in the first sleep cycle.
REM rebound occurs equally in all cycles.
REM rebound is absent in recovery sleep.

questions.explanation: REM rebound is most prominent later in the night. It is not limited to the first cycle, evenly distributed, or absent.
questions.hint: When in the night is REM rebound strongest?

questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: What the Body Does While Asleep
questions.stem: Marine biologist Abel asks how sleep supports immune function.

answer.exemplar: Sleep promotes cytokine release and immune cell activity; sleep loss reduces antibody response and increases infection susceptibility.

questions.explanation: Sleep enhances cytokine production and immune cell function. Sleep loss impairs antibody responses and raises infection risk.
questions.hint: Connect sleep to cytokine and antibody responses.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Whether Sleep Consolidates What Was Learned
questions.stem: A sleep group scores 90 on a memory test; a wake group scores 60. What is the ratio of sleep to wake scores?
questions.explanation: Divide sleep by wake: 90 / 60 = 1.5. The sleep group scored 1.5 times the wake group.
questions.hint: Divide 90 by 60.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Cases Per Thousand People and Cases Per Thousand Years
questions.stem: Marine biologist Bianca must choose the right measure for a sleep disorder in a population.

options.text: Use incidence to describe how many currently have the disorder.
options.misconception: incidence measures new cases, not current cases

options.text: Use mortality to describe how many sleep poorly.
options.misconception: mortality measures deaths, not sleep quality

options.text: Use prevalence to describe how many currently have the disorder.
Use relative risk to describe current case counts.
options.misconception: relative risk compares groups, not counts

questions.explanation: Prevalence describes current cases. Incidence, mortality, and relative risk answer different questions.
questions.hint: Which measure counts current cases?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Ratios From a Study That Chose Its Groups
questions.learningObjective: Identify a limitation of odds ratios
questions.stem: Marine biologist Cato asks when an odds ratio poorly approximates relative risk.

options.text: When the study is randomized.
options.misconception: randomization does not affect OR-RR approximation

options.text: When the outcome is very rare.
options.misconception: rare outcomes make OR approximate RR well

options.text: When the sample size is large.
options.misconception: large samples improve precision, not approximation

options.text: When the outcome is common in the population.

questions.explanation: Odds ratios approximate relative risk well only when outcomes are rare. Common outcomes inflate the odds ratio relative to risk.
questions.hint: When does OR diverge from RR?

questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Two Systems That Set the Time of Sleep
questions.stem: Marine biologist Dara reads a graph showing sleep propensity rising with wakefulness and dipping with circadian alertness in the evening.

options.text: Sleep propensity is driven only by circadian alertness.
Sleep propensity falls as wakefulness increases.
Sleep propensity reflects both rising homeostatic pressure and circadian modulation.
Circadian alertness promotes sleep in the evening.

questions.explanation: Sleep propensity combines rising homeostatic pressure with circadian modulation. Neither process alone explains the graph.
questions.hint: Which option combines both processes?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Self-Report Against Task Performance During Sleep Restriction
questions.stem: Marine biologist Elia asks why PVT lapses increase disproportionately during sleep restriction.

answer.exemplar: Sleep loss impairs sustained attention and slows responses; lapses reflect microsleeps and attentional failures that grow nonlinearly with restriction.

questions.explanation: Sleep restriction causes attentional failures and microsleeps. Lapses grow nonlinearly because sustained attention is highly sleep-sensitive.
questions.hint: Connect sleep loss to attentional failures.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Whether Recovery Sleep Restores Everything
questions.stem: A recovery night allows 480 minutes in bed and 432 minutes of sleep. What is the sleep efficiency percentage?
questions.explanation: Sleep efficiency = 432 / 480 * 100 = 90 percent. Recovery sleep is typically efficient.
questions.hint: Divide 432 by 480 and multiply by 100.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: A Night Without Dreaming After a Week Without Sleep
questions.stem: Marine biologist Fara must summarize the effects of a week of REM deprivation followed by recovery sleep.

options.text: REM deprivation has no effects and rebound never occurs.
Recovery sleep contains less REM than baseline.
REM deprivation permanently eliminates REM sleep.
REM deprivation increases REM pressure, producing rebound with vivid dreams.

questions.explanation: REM deprivation builds homeostatic pressure, leading to rebound with increased, vivid REM in recovery. Permanent loss, no effect, or reduced REM are incorrect.
questions.hint: Which option captures pressure buildup and rebound?
